title: Mothers in Mannu's prison
hook: the Ardas remembers Sikh women imprisoned with their children who kept faith

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ala Singh and Patiala: a fort, a well, a town beginning. Your line was towns begin. What did you learn about where you live? Today, a harder story, told gently. Day eight hundred seventy-three.

In gurdwaras, a congregation stands, and someone leads the Ardas, the prayer that remembers the community's history out loud. Part of it calls to mind people who suffered and kept their faith. Among them are women, the Singhnian. Not named one by one. Remembered together. Tradition places them in a prison in Lahore, under a governor named Mir Mannu, with their children beside them. This is a heavy story, and it's told here carefully. Today: mothers in Mannu's prison.
screen: `THE ARDAS, SAID STANDING.` → `IT REMEMBERS SIKH WOMEN, TOGETHER.` → `A PRISON IN LAHORE.`

segments.voice: Here is what tradition says happened. In the hard years, the governor at Lahore, Mir Mannu, had Sikh women seized from villages and held in prison with their small children. They were set to grind grain on heavy hand mills, with little to eat. And they were told there was a way out: give up the Sikh faith. Tradition says they refused. That's the first thing. The second is how they endured. Tradition says that while they ground the grain, they recited the Guru's hymns, the words keeping time with the stone. Whatever else was taken, the words stayed with them. The third thing is the worst part, and Sikh memory doesn't hide it. Tradition says their children were killed in front of them, and still they did not give up their faith. The Ardas remembers Singhnian, Sikh women, beside the men who gave their lives and did not give up their faith, and some who lead it add words for the mothers whose children were killed before them. It isn't said for shock. It's said so that no one forgets what was carried. The fourth thing is where they are remembered now. In Lahore, a place called the Shaheed Ganj of the Singhnian, Sikh women, marks the memory. And when the Ardas is said, in a village gurdwara or a great one, these women are in the room. Their story is not kept as a tale of what was done to them. It is kept as a tale of what they held on to. The mothers kept faith.
screen: `SEIZED, IMPRISONED, TOLD TO GIVE UP.` · `GRINDING GRAIN, RECITING THE HYMNS.` · `THE CHILDREN, AND STILL THEY KEPT FAITH.` · `REMEMBERED WHEN THE ARDAS IS SAID.` · then, large: `THE MOTHERS KEPT FAITH.`

segments.voice: For this sit, hold mothers in hardship. Breathe slowly. Bring to mind any mother, anywhere, carrying more than she should have to: in a war, in a hospital corridor, in a prison visiting room, at a kitchen table with a pile of bills. You don't need to know her. Just hold her in mind, with her children. If you pray, you can pray for her in your own way, or say Waheguru on each breath out. If you don't, simply hold her there. The bell holds the time.

Singhnian, the Sikh women remembered beside the men in the Ardas. Tradition says they were held with their children in Lahore, and ground grain, recited the hymns, and did not give up their faith. Today's word.
Your line: the mothers kept faith. Today, do one kind thing for a mother you know, or for someone mothering others: a call, a meal, an hour of help. Day eight hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Sikh women who kept their faith are remembered when the Ardas is said, standing, at the end of services and at many daily and family occasions; a site in Lahore also keeps their memory.
